h: The SIR tangle: it cannot be fixed, it has to be scrapped
dek: Three former senior officials use sections of the law and figures from the ground to explain why the Special Intensive Revision of the voter list is wrong at its very foundation.
by: N.K. Sharma, Sanjay Kumar and Siraj Hussain
body: On Delhi's streets the demand is for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign. But N.K. Sharma and Sanjay Kumar, both retired from the statistics ministry, and former Union agriculture secretary Siraj Hussain say the problem is bigger than one chair. In their view the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) has become a national disaster, and in the end more than 15 crore eligible citizens could be left off the list. The article does not explain how this estimate was reached.

The first mistake is treating the old, error-filled 2002-03 rolls as if they were set in stone. The second lies in how the 'shifted elsewhere' voter is understood. Section 20(1A) of the Representation of the People Act 1950 says that being away for some time does not end a person's ordinary residence. According to the authors, most names were struck off because of this wrong reading.

The third issue is the hearing. Lakhs of names were removed without notice, even though the Supreme Court, in the 1995 Lal Babu Hussein judgment, said notice is required before a name is deleted. Form 7 was also misused: in Karnataka 91,278 such forms were filed between June and October, and in Uttar Pradesh 85,854 names were deleted on bulk applications after the deadline had passed.

The fifth mistake is the 'logical discrepancy' software, which flags spelling differences, the ages of parents and children, or having more than five siblings. The authors say none of this has anything to do with being a voter. In Bengal the notices were concentrated in Muslim-majority districts, and in Nandigram 95 per cent of the voters removed are Muslim, though they make up about 25 per cent of the population.

The Commission says those left out can fill Form 6. The authors reply that after the 2022 amendment this form is only for people registering for the first time. So their demand is clear: scrap the SIR, restore the earlier rolls, and if there is any revision in future, do it with full consultation. They call it an NRC brought in through the back door.
nazar: This article takes the movement beyond slogans and puts it on the ground of law and paperwork. The 'discrepancies' for which names are being cut, a spelling slip, a large family, moving cities for work, are the ordinary lives of poor families, migrant workers, Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities) and Muslims. The rule looks the same for everyone, but it does not hit everyone the same way.
Whether Gyanesh Kumar goes or stays, if the list stays the same, those who lost their rights will not get them back. Perhaps the movement's most solid demand is this: first the list, then the chair.
sawal: Should a software 'discrepancy' decide whether someone gets to vote?
ref: Form 7
An application to object to a name on the voter list or to have it removed. Any voter can file it, which is why there is a fear of bulk misuse.
Lal Babu Hussein case (1995)
A Supreme Court ruling that before a name is removed on suspicion, the person must get notice and a chance to be heard.
ank: eligible citizens who could be left off the list
share of Muslims among voters removed in Nandigram

h: Apoorvanand: the fear is broken, now it is the institutions' turn
dek: In Navjivan, Apoorvanand argues that between July and October the government's legitimacy has taken such a blow that the media, the bureaucracy and the courts must now pick a side.
body: Apoorvanand, who teaches at Delhi University, says that for three months people have been asking him the same question: does protest change anything? In July, after thousands of young people from across the country gathered at Jantar Mantar, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan had to go, and the claim that 'nobody resigns in this government' became a joke. According to the author, the public saw it simply as the government bending before resistance.

He places this in a line of older movements. Farmers sat at Delhi's borders for a year and got three laws withdrawn, which in his view was a bigger defeat, because policy changed. The anti-CAA movement led by Muslim women got the rules postponed and the NRC put on the back burner. The difference is that this time the young people did not raise markers of identity that could make any group feel left out, so the support is far wider than before.

According to the author, Jantar Mantar dented the image of the 'supreme' leader more deeply than any earlier movement, and then the Indian Express investigation into the Election Commission almost brought down the government's legitimacy. That is why people no longer see the current protests as the work of any one party. For the first time in thirteen years, the government looks alone and on the defensive.

He warns that a politically weakened government has given the agencies a free hand. Citing reports, he alleges that Delhi Police is spreading misinformation against the protests, which is outside its remit. The question is whether the courts will act independently.

His conclusion is that people's fear has broken and they are now taking back the right to protest without asking permission. The structure of power that stands on the media, corporations and the judiciary is shaking from these blows, and these institutions have to decide whether they will free themselves or become partners in its fall.
nazar: Apoorvanand's most useful point is that this time the movement did not put any identity in front, and that is why it was hard to set it against majoritarian anger. We should also remember that the Muslim women who opened this path against the CAA paid the biggest price for it. The allegation is that the poor, migrants and minorities make up most of the names that were cut, so the test of this new unity will be whether it lasts until their names are restored.
sawal: Will the institutions let go of fear, the way the public has?
ref: Indian Express investigation
A September 2026 report that detailed the written objections of two election commissioners. The Commission called the disagreement normal.
CAA-NRC movement
The 2019-20 protests, best known for the sit-in by Muslim women at Shaheen Bagh.

h: Moving the venue does not change the voice
dek: A Siasat editorial: removing Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites is less an administrative decision and more a strategy to crush the protest against Gyanesh Kumar.
photo_note: Representative image: the Jantar Mantar observatory
body: Hyderabad's Urdu newspaper Siasat opens this editorial with a couplet whose meaning is that people with self-respect do not write odes in praise of the ruler. Then it comes straight to the point: the central government is afraid of the protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and its every step shows this fear. Thousands of barricades, detentions, and hours of driving people around in buses: the paper sees this as panic.

The editorial recalls that Jantar Mantar has for years been the designated place for protest in Delhi. It was from here that the Cockroach Janata Party movement spread across the country and, according to the paper, Dharmendra Pradhan had to leave the education ministry. Now, when the CJP, AISA, other student groups, citizens' groups and lawyers announced a sit-in here against Gyanesh Kumar, the police threw in their full force, detained thousands and then turned Jantar Mantar itself into a protest-free zone. Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and the CBD Ground were offered as alternatives.

The paper accepts that legally the Centre or Delhi Police can decide protest sites. But its question is about timing: why this sudden decision right in the middle of this movement? According to the editorial, there is no other reason in sight except that the government wants to keep citizens away from their constitutional right to peaceful protest.

The sharpest point is the comparison the editorial makes. In its view, just as 13 crore people were stripped of their right to vote in the name of the SIR, the right to protest is now being attacked in the same way. This figure and allegation are repeated constantly by the movement, and the paper makes them the basis of its argument.

In the end the editorial says that changing the venue will neither end the movement nor weaken it. Students, young people, lawyers and citizens' organisations are on the streets, and the government should understand that this voice cannot be suppressed.
nazar: Jantar Mantar is a kilometre or a kilometre and a half from Parliament; Burari and Karkardooma are fifteen to twenty kilometres away. For a workers', farmers' or Dalit group that has neither media nor a big crowd, this distance makes the difference: near Parliament even a hundred people made news, while outside the city even a thousand can go unseen. The right to vote and the right to protest are a pair, and Siasat is right that both are being hit at once.
sawal: If the protest site is far away, who gets heard?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision: a fresh check of the voter list. It is alleged that crores of names were cut in it.
Protest site notification
A standing order of Delhi Police that sets where protests can be held. Jantar Mantar is now off this list.

h: Will a police station now decide who is a journalist?
dek: The Quint's video journalist Sarthak Jaiswal uses his five-hour detention to ask why the police are picking and choosing the witnesses.
body: At about nine in the morning on 10 October, Sarthak Jaiswal and Queerbeat journalist Anureet Watta set out to record the protest. Around 50 metro stations in the city were shut, railway stations locked, roads barricaded, cab apps down and the internet off. They were stopped near Ashoka Police Lane. Both had press cards, but the officer insisted on a PIB card.

The two were taken to Chanakyapuri police station for 'verification', where they were asked for their names, phone numbers, father's name, Aadhaar and home address. They said their identity could be checked with their office or from their cards, and were told there was no internet. For about five hours they were not even told clearly whether they were in detention or not, and in the end they had to hand over their Aadhaar to be released.

Jaiswal's argument goes beyond this personal story. When the police start deciding who is a real journalist, what they are really deciding is who gets to witness the protest and which picture reaches the public. In his view, the insistence on a PIB card is an attempt to filter information through a single government window.

He believes independent digital and regional media have loosened the hold of the government's and big channels' version of events, and that this is the root of the irritation. It also bothers him that pushing and shoving journalists is now treated as a routine part of the job. At the station, the other detainees were being lectured as if they had been misled, while the journalists were treated more gently. He reads a difference of class and caste in this too.
nazar: A journalist with a big office and lawyers behind them gets out in five hours. For an independent reporter from a small town, a Dalit or Muslim journalist, or a YouTuber with no institution, the same questioning can become weeks of trouble. Asking for Aadhaar and a father's name looks less like checking identity and more like building a surveillance file.
sawal: If the witnesses themselves are removed, who will record the truth?
ref: PIB card
Accreditation given by the central government's Press Information Bureau. Most independent and digital journalists do not have it.

h: Fear on guard in the capital: a panicked government, fearless young people
dek: The Wire's newsletter records Delhi on 10 October as an armed camp and says this is a sign not of strength but of panic.
body: The India Cable opens with a sharp charge: on 10 October the government went to war against its own citizens. New Delhi became a camp ringed with barricades, and according to the newsletter the security forces seemed to be guarding those in power, not the public. Citing PTI, more than 7,000 people were detained that day.

The piece lists the detentions at length. The CJP's Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were taken off an Air India flight; Dipke's 85-year-old grandmother had died that same morning. Mamata Banerjee, Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Manik Sarkar were detained. Neha Bora, Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were picked up near Dilli Haat, and Dhruv Rathee was taken from his home in Gurugram.

There is special focus on journalists. According to the piece, reporters were held even after showing press cards, Newslaundry staff were told they were not media, and Scroll's political editor Shoaib Daniyal was picked up while waiting for a taxi away from the protest. Near the Supreme Court, senior advocate Shadan Farasat was dragged, and around 100 lawyers were taken to the Yamuna Sports Complex.

The UN human rights office also asked for the release of those detained without reason. The newsletter concludes that Delhi Police has begun to look like a police state and that the government is rattled by a generation demanding accountability. At the end it records the CJP's Ajinkya Shinde announcing a march towards Jantar Mantar every day until the resignation, which means the attempt to intimidate is backfiring.
nazar: The strength of this piece is its list. When former chief ministers, lawyers, journalists and students are all packed into buses the same way on a single day, the question is no longer about law and order but about the right to dissent.

We should also remember that behind these familiar names were thousands of others, students from small towns, workers, young Dalits and Muslims, whose detention never makes news and for whom no lawyer stands outside the police station all night.
sawal: Who will finally account for seven thousand detentions?
ref: The India Cable
A daily newsletter linked to The Wire that presents the day's news with commentary.
OHCHR
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, which monitors human rights violations around the world.

h: TV showed the police, newspapers showed the protest
dek: Shailaja Bajpai's media column shows how incompletely the story of 10 October reached viewers on the channels.
body: The CJP protest dominated newspapers, TV, digital and social media for about 72 hours, but according to Shailaja Bajpai each medium showed a different Delhi. Even before the protest, there were reports of 45,000 security personnel, 45 closed metro stations, halted trains and the internet shut down. By evening, newspapers were counting up to 7,000 detentions.

Bajpai writes that channels like Aaj Tak, India Today, NDTV, Times Now, India TV and News18 focused on the police presence, on everything being normal and on the protest having failed. Both Republic channels were openly against the protesters. The scene of CJP leaders being taken off a plane ran a lot, because it had spectacle.

What was left out mattered more: the detention of lawyers near the Supreme Court, AISA's protest at Dilli Haat, and the incident at Connaught Place in which right-wing group members allegedly beat protesters in front of the police. The detention of journalists from Navbharat Times, Scroll and Newslaundry was printed in newspapers but barely appeared on TV. Only India Today showed the CJP's press conference on Sunday.

The newspapers told a different story. The Sunday Times of India gave it eight pages, others three to five, and the Sunday Express lead tied the lockdown and the crackdown together. The column's takeaway is that the story was too big to be buried, but the TV frame cut off half of it.
nazar: In a country where most people get their news on TV and mobile phones, the picture of 'peace prevailed, protest flopped' becomes the truth for many. The village or small-town voter whose name was cut from the list is not told by the channels that this movement is really about their own vote.
sawal: What did you see on 10 October, and on which screen?
ref: Tele-Scope
Shailaja Bajpai's regular column in ThePrint that examines TV news and media coverage.

h: No party flags, only the tricolour: Siasat on the INDIA bloc march
dek: Siasat's second editorial says Monday's march was bigger than party politics, but keeping the movement peaceful and guarding it from infiltration is now the biggest responsibility.
body: This editorial also begins with a couplet, meaning roughly: we know well what is good and bad for us, since when did you become a teacher of morals? It seems aimed at critics who are attacking the opposition for taking to the streets, though the paper names no one.

According to Siasat, lakhs of people joined the march held in Delhi on Monday by the INDIA alliance, led by the Congress, against alleged vote theft. This crowd did not come out of nowhere: the protests going on since 2 October, the turning of Jantar Mantar into a police camp, the failed attempt to reach the Commission's office, the tribute at Rajghat and the rally a day earlier are all links in this chain. AISA president Neha Bora and workers from many organisations also took part. The paper concludes that this has become not just a political fight but the fight of almost every major section of society.

The editorial's central claim is that people now understand their votes really were being stolen. In its view, the cutting of 13 crore names in the SIR is no accident but a deliberate conspiracy to impose a particular ideology. This is the paper's allegation. It also warns that in states where the SIR is still under way or yet to happen, this number could grow.

The paper puts special stress on one detail: there was no party flag in the march, only the tricolour. In its eyes this is proof that the fight belongs not to any one party but to people's democratic rights.

In the end the editorial sounds a warning. It alleges that thugs were planted to disrupt the march and failed, but that there will be more such attempts. The movement must stay peaceful and must not let anyone use it, because its real capital is the people's trust.
nazar: Raising the tricolour is wise, but the fact that a Muslim newspaper from Hyderabad stresses that the fight is not about any identity says something in itself: the groups most afraid of having their names cut know how easy it is to single them out and target them. The appeal for peace also comes from this experience. The blame for any violence lands first on the weakest.
sawal: Will opposition unity hold from the street to Parliament?
ref: INDIA alliance
A front of opposition parties including the Congress, which led a march to the Supreme Court on 12 October.
AISA
All India Students' Association, a left student organisation. Its president Neha Bora is a well-known face of this movement.

h: Why shut down a city of two crore for one official?
dek: Akhlaq Siddiqui links the scenes from Washington to Delhi and asks: if the list is clean, why fear an audit?
body: The piece begins in Washington, where a few dozen supporters of the Indian Overseas Congress and Hindus for Human Rights gathered in the rain near the Gandhi statue on Massachusetts Avenue. Their allegation was that in India the courts put off election disputes and getting deleted names restored is slow and expensive. The government rejects these allegations.

Then Siddiqui sets out the Delhi account: about 25,000 police and paramilitary personnel, trains into New Delhi stopped, mobile internet cut in the central area, dozens of metro stations and markets shut. Detention figures vary. Reuters, citing a home ministry official, put it at about 2,000; The Hindu, citing police sources, at about 2,500.

The piece recalls that the very next day Jantar Mantar lost its status as a protest site, and Ramlila Maidan, Burari and the CBD Ground in east Delhi were suggested instead. When the UN human rights office and Amnesty raised concerns, India's mission in Geneva called it interference in internal matters.

Siddiqui accepts that no government can let a crowd decide when and where it gathers, and that July's violence can also be cited. But his question is that leaving the voter list dispute unresolved and shutting down a city of two crore people to protect one election official does not show confidence. He has three suggestions: make the deletion figures public, open a route for appeal, and hold an independent audit. If the list is clean, the audit will prove it.
nazar: Without taking the movement's side, this piece arrives at the same demand that is on the street: show the numbers. Most of those whose names were cut have no lawyer, no time to run around offices and no bundle of papers. For them an audit is not just a question of transparency but the way to get their vote back.
sawal: If the list is clean, why the hesitation to put out the figures?
ref: Denotify
To withdraw a status a place got through a government notification, such as being a designated protest site.

h: From Boat Club to Burari: dissent pushed ever further from power
dek: In Prabhasakshi, Mahendra Tiwari takes stock of 33 years of Jantar Mantar and asks whether a protest sent 15-20 kilometres away can reach the government at all.
photo_note: Representative image: one of the instruments at Jantar Mantar
body: Mahendra Tiwari sees Jantar Mantar as more than an eighteenth-century observatory. In his view, from 1993 to 2026, that is for 33 years, the place was a laboratory of India's social and political movements. After a high-level committee's recommendation to the home ministry, Delhi Police changed its April 2022 standing order and removed Jantar Mantar from the list of authorised protest sites. Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and the CBD Ground at Karkardooma were named in its place.

The author lists the site's legacy: the 2011 Lokpal movement, the anger after Nirbhaya in 2012, the One Rank One Pension sit-in by ex-servicemen in 2015 and the women wrestlers' struggle in 2023. Farmers, workers, students, teachers and marginalised groups spoke to power from here, because Parliament is just a kilometre or a kilometre and a half away.

He also sets out the government's arguments. More than one lakh people came to the student movement that ran for about 36 days in June-July 2026, far beyond the site's capacity, and there were clashes when they moved towards Parliament. According to the author, 118 police personnel and dozens of students were injured. There is also the argument about traffic and business.

But the article's real argument is about distance. In 1988, when lakhs of farmers with Mahendra Singh Tikait held out at Boat Club for a week, protests there were stopped. In 2017 the National Green Tribunal put partial curbs on Jantar Mantar, and now it is out altogether. According to the author, this sequence shows the growing physical and mental distance between citizen and power: at Jantar Mantar even a hundred people became a national debate, while at Burari and Karkardooma it will be easy to ignore dissent.

He recalls Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b), and the Supreme Court's point in the 2018 Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan case that the right to protest cannot be made meaningless in the name of law and order. The venue may change; the government's willingness to listen should not.
nazar: Prabhasakshi is generally seen as close to the government, which makes this article's argument about distance all the more significant. Sending protest out of the city hurts most those who have no TV cameras, only their presence: contract workers, displaced Adivasis, Dalit groups, ASHA and anganwadi (village health and childcare) workers. When names are allegedly being cut from the voter list and the place to complain is also moved far away, the door to speaking up in a democracy narrows from both sides.
sawal: How much of a sit-in at Burari will be heard in Parliament?
ref: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan vs Union of India (2018)
The Supreme Court said protests at Jantar Mantar and Boat Club cannot be banned completely, and a balance is needed.
Boat Club
The grounds near India Gate, the main site for big protests in Delhi until 1988.

h: A second look: why rush to the camera before the court decides?
dek: In The Dossier, Akanksha Singh Raghuvanshi argues that the opposition's march to the Supreme Court made pictures, while the real fight lies in the petition filed in court.
body: This is a piece critical of the movement. The writer begins with the 12 October march in which Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi walked towards the Supreme Court with AISA president Neha Bora. Their memorandum had four demands: end "vote theft", the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a halt to the SIR and a return to paper ballots. According to the writer, Chief Justice Surya Kant declined to meet them and said such matters were listed for the next day.

She says the real step that day was the joint writ petition filed by Rahul Gandhi and ten other leaders: it asks for the Commission's files, minutes of meetings and database access logs, and for the deletions to be examined by a committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge. In the writer's view, the march only added pictures. The paper-ballot demand also clashes with the Supreme Court's April 2024 ruling.

On the numbers, the writer sets out the Commission's side. The opposition speaks of 13 crore names cut; the Commission says that out of 95.40 crore entries checked in three phases, 13.39 crore were found absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, and that about 2.73 crore new voters aged 18 to 28 were added. The writer says these figures can be checked, so "vote theft" is for now a disputed number, not a proven fact.

She accepts that the court is serious. On 5 October the bench issued notice, said it had never approved the modified Form 6, and asked to see whether the decisions were taken by all three commissioners or by Gyanesh Kumar alone. There are also reports of objections by commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.

Her conclusion is that the SIR needs scrutiny and the Commission must show its working, but street pressure turns a legal question into a contest of endurance. If the court finds that Form 6 was changed by one man, the opposition will get a judgment, which no march can give.
nazar: This is the most measured argument from the other side, and so it is worth reading. But it misses something big: of the 13 crore entries the Commission calls a clean-up, every wrong deletion could be a poor, migrant, Dalit or Muslim voter who has neither the time nor the papers to fill the form again. The matter reached the court only because pressure built on the street; in April, the notice for removal was not even allowed to be admitted in Parliament.
The street and the court are not opposites. When the dissent of two commissioners stays buried and even Jantar Mantar is shut, saying "wait for the verdict" helps those who have both time and power.
sawal: Must one wait for a verdict in silence?
ref: Form 6
The form to add a new name to the voter list. It is alleged that it was changed without Parliament's approval.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision: a nationwide re-check of voter lists, accused of cutting names on a large scale.

h: A barricade is a tool of order, not a wall against democracy
dek: In Times Now Navbharat, Sunil Kumar Sirij asks whether five days in custody was really needed for CJP leaders who entered Jantar Mantar with the tricolour.
body: The writer's basic test is that a democracy is not judged by how easily it can stop dissent, but by how well it balances protest, law and accountability. He holds the latest events at Jantar Mantar up to this test.

After Jantar Mantar was dropped from the list of protest sites, Delhi Police named Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground as the new venues. The writer argues that sending protest far from Parliament keeps the right alive on paper but cuts its reach and visibility. On 13 October Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and others crossed barricades and closed gates to get inside; the next day both were sent to five days of judicial custody. Police have charged them with trespass, breaking prohibitory orders, violating peace bonds and obstructing public servants.

The writer accepts that the right to protest is not unlimited, and that breaking a valid restriction can lead to legal action. But 'law and order' cannot by itself justify every restriction. Each one must pass three questions: is there a real need, is the restriction in proportion to that need, and could a softer step have worked.

He also says charges must be weighed person by person, on evidence and recordings; treating everyone alike is wrong, and a police accusation is not a final verdict. The CJP legal team's claim that the leaders were kept from their lawyers late into the night should be checked independently, along with whether the arrest was properly notified, families were contacted and procedure followed.

Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) guarantee speech and peaceful assembly; 19(2) and 19(3) allow reasonable restrictions. The writer concludes that custody must be lawful and no wider than needed, and that barricades should stay tools of order, not become a wall standing in front of democracy.
nazar: This measured piece on the website of a mainstream Hindi TV channel matters because it offers not a slogan for the movement but a constitutional test, and five days in jail does not seem to pass that test. Even if climbing a gate with the tricolour is an offence, jail cannot be the punishment before any trial.

The real question is one the writer raises but does not fully open: who decided to drop Jantar Mantar from the list, on what need, and when. Until that is answered, protest sent off to grounds on the city's edge is a kind of exile.
sawal: How much of a protest remains once it is sent away from Parliament?
ref: Article 19(1)(b)
The part of the Constitution that gives citizens the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. Article 19(3) allows reasonable limits on it.
Proportionality
A test courts use: any limit on a right must match the need, go no further, and be the least harsh option available.

h: Kamal Mitra Chenoy: secularism is not a concession, it is a condition of democracy
dek: In ThePrint, Vitasta Kaul remembers how this JNU political scientist made fighting communalism his life's work after 1984.
body: Former JNU professor Kamal Mitra Chenoy died in Delhi on 10 October at the age of 75. According to his family, he was diagnosed with fast-progressing Alzheimer's in 2020, and the Covid years made his condition worse. Vitasta Kaul's tribute ties his life together with one thread: for him, secularism was not a favour done to minorities but the basic condition for democracy to survive.

Born in 1950, Chenoy went to the Indian Military Academy for a short while after the Doon School, but came back within three months. In 1969, while studying economics at Kirori Mal College, he joined student politics and the AISF, the CPI's student wing. In 1972 he reached JNU, where its debates shaped him. He later taught comparative politics and the Constitution at its School of International Studies and retired in 2018.

According to the article, the turning point came on 1 November 1984, when he went around Delhi in the middle of the anti-Sikh violence. After that experience he resolved to fight communalism. Later, after the violence in Meerut, Ayodhya, Gujarat and Muzaffarnagar, he joined fact-finding teams and people's tribunals, met victims and challenged the stories that hid the responsibility of those in power.

He argued that the majority is not one uniform community; it too is divided by caste, class, gender, language and region. Defining the country by one religious identity would hollow out the very plurality on which Indian democracy stands. After Gujarat 2002 he wrote that an attack on secularism is really an attack on democracy.

He was in the CPI for nearly four decades, joined the Aam Aadmi Party in 2014 and later left it too, but never broke with the Left. Before MGNREGA (the rural job guarantee scheme) came in, he went on a 53-day bus journey with Jean Dreze and Annie Raja. His old friend Anand K. Sahay remembers him as a soft-hearted man, a romantic poet and a revolutionary.
nazar: Chenoy's biggest legacy is the understanding that protecting minorities, Dalits and weaker sections is not some 'special arrangement' apart from democracy; it is democracy's real test. The tradition of fact-finding that he strengthened is the one under the most pressure today, and keeping it alive would be the truest tribute to him.
sawal: Is there still room today for fact-finding teams?
ref: Fact-finding mission
An independent inquiry by citizens' groups after violence or repression, in which a report is prepared after meeting victims and witnesses.
People's tribunal
A hearing like a people's court, where judges, scholars and activists hear testimony and give public findings; it has no legal force.

h: The debater of Ganga Dhaba, who stayed a student to the end
dek: On Counterview, Harsh Thakor remembers Kamal Mitra Chenoy as a scholar who was present equally in the classroom and on the street.
body: This article by independent journalist Harsh Thakor stresses the side of Kamal Mitra Chenoy's life that set him apart from other professors: he kept teaching and also remained a student activist. According to the article, he died of internal bleeding after being diagnosed with Alzheimer's in 2020 and getting Covid three times in 2021-22. He is survived by his wife, Professor Anuradha M. Chenoy, and their children Ayesha and Ajit.

Chenoy was born in Delhi in 1950. His father was in the foreign service, and his mother, Shanta Chenoy, came from a Baghdadi Jewish family. In 1969 he was elected to the executive of the Delhi University Students' Union, and in 1973 he became secretary of the AISF. At JNU he was vice-president of the students' union and later also president of the teachers' association.

Colleagues remember his weekly debates with students at Ganga Dhaba. He was in the CPI for a long time, but made decisions in his own way. Peace with neighbours including Pakistan, solidarity with Palestine and opposition to nuclear weapons were his lasting concerns. In 2006, when Medha Patkar was detained while on a hunger strike against Sardar Sarovar, Chenoy also kept a four-day fast.

As a scholar, his question was: who really benefits from development? In his 1993 book 'Sustainable Development in India: A Radical View', he criticised the single, Western-path model of the IMF and the World Bank. According to the author, he believed that India has no single majority, only many minorities, and that the politics of majoritarianism rests on an illusion.

The article also records his three decades of fact-finding work and his role at the 2004 World Social Forum, where he said it was wrong to treat GDP growth as real development. The sense of one colleague's words is that to remember him is to remember a JNU that may never come back.
nazar: Chenoy's thinking on development is as necessary today: when dams, mines and 'development' projects uproot Adivasis (indigenous communities) and farmers, asking who benefited should be the first question of politics. With the passing of his generation, which saw the university as an open space for debate, the responsibility grows to make sure that room for dissent survives on campus.
sawal: Are debates like those at Ganga Dhaba possible on today's campuses?
ref: Sardar Sarovar
A large dam on the Narmada. The Narmada Bachao Andolan fought for decades for the rights of the people it displaced.
World Social Forum
An annual gathering of movements looking for alternatives to globalisation; in 2004 it was held in Mumbai.

h: Israel's election race: who will be harsher on Palestinians
dek: In an Al Jazeera analysis, Urooba Jamal shows that Israel's 27 October election is not a call for change but a deepening of post-war hardline nationalism.
body: Israel votes on 27 October, and Urooba Jamal's analysis says the Gaza war has now become the centre of its domestic politics. In the view of the analysts she spoke to, this election is less a call for change and more a confirmation of the hardline nationalism that rose after 7 October 2023. Questions like a Palestinian state have almost vanished from the mainstream debate.

Netanyahu's whole campaign rests on the claim that only he can keep Israelis safe. According to reports, he received warnings of an attack from Egypt and the UAE in 2023, which he denies. His opponents call him 'unfit', but the polls show little effect.

The article gives a long list of far-right statements: Finance Minister Smotrich saying the West Bank should get the same as Gaza, demands to annex Gaza, and several parties backing the expulsion of Palestinians. According to analyst Ahmad Najjar, this is an election message that presents Palestinians as a population problem, and the race is over who will wipe out their lives most brutally.

The figures show the cost of this race: more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, and about 1,500 have died even after last year's 'ceasefire'. The number of settlers in the West Bank has grown from about 2.6 lakh (260,000) in 1993 to more than 7 lakh (700,000). Meanwhile, Sami Abu Shehadeh, a citizen of Palestinian origin, had to drop out of the race over his comments on Gaza, while no curbs were placed on the far right.

The general view of the analysts is that the two-state solution is not even under discussion right now; no Jewish Zionist party is putting it forward. According to Ahron Bregman, bringing it back would need heavy international pressure and non-violent resistance. And even if Netanyahu loses, people in Lebanon and Syria do not expect any big difference.
nazar: This analysis is a reminder that the politics of occupation does not change when one leader goes, if the whole electoral field runs on presenting another community as a threat. In India too, language that calls minorities a 'population problem' has been a tool to win elections, so for people here who care about democracy this is not distant news but a warning. Questioning the Indian government's growing closeness to Israel is part of this.
sawal: Will anything change for Palestinians even after Netanyahu?
ref: Two-state solution
The proposal to create a sovereign Palestinian state alongside Israel, which has been the basis of international diplomacy for decades.
Dahiya doctrine
An Israeli military policy of heavy, disproportionate attacks on civilian infrastructure; the name comes from the Dahiya area of Beirut.

h: Repression does not bring stability: Maleeha Lodhi's advice to Pakistan
dek: In Dawn, former ambassador Maleeha Lodhi writes that governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the crackdown on the opposition will make the country more unstable.
body: In Pakistan, the confrontation has sharpened again after talks broke down between the PTI and the federal government. Maleeha Lodhi, who has been ambassador to the US, the UK and the United Nations, explains that to stop the PTI's march, the Shehbaz Sharif government first threatened to remove the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government and then imposed an emergency and governor's rule there. In her view the most serious step is the alleged picking up of more than eight PTI legislators, who are being held without contact.

Lodhi sees this as a repeat of an old pattern, but in a deepening authoritarian climate. In the last couple of years, bans on rallies, crushing protests, cases against critics, surveillance of the media, internet shutdowns and criminalising free speech have become common. Judicial independence has been weakened through disputed amendments and by ignoring court orders. In her words, only the shell of democracy is left.

She accepts that earlier civilian governments also jailed opponents and pressed down on the press, but the scale of today's crackdown is far bigger, especially in digital censorship. Her central argument is that repression is a sign of weakness, not strength. Force can bring calm on the surface, but it deepens polarisation and hollows out the social contract.

It has an economic cost too: repeated blockades of cities scare off business and investment, just when the economy's recovery is weak. Celebrating IMF instalments is no guarantee of lasting growth, and surveys show growing despair among people.

The way forward she suggests: talks that lead to a lasting settlement, treating Imran Khan as the court orders say and letting opposition leaders consult him, an end to 'winner takes all' thinking, working together with opposition-ruled provinces, and stronger institutions.
nazar: This crisis next door is a mirror for India: sidelining an elected provincial government, detaining opposition leaders and shutting down the internet are becoming a shared grammar of power in South Asia. The heaviest blow of such repression always falls on ordinary people, workers and minorities in border areas, who have neither a voice nor access to the courts.
sawal: Have South Asia's governments come to treat repression as governance?
ref: Governor's rule
Removing a provincial government and handing administration directly to a governor appointed by the centre, somewhat like President's Rule in India.
PTI
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, Imran Khan's party, which was in power in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

h: When will Bangladesh's wait for press freedom end?
dek: In The Daily Star, Prothom Alo editor Matiur Rahman asks why student demands made in 1962 remain unmet 64 years later.
body: This article by Matiur Rahman, editor and publisher of Prothom Alo, Bangladesh's largest newspaper, is a slightly shortened version of his speech at the 'Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026' in Dhaka. He begins with 1 February 1962, when Dhaka University students went on strike against Pakistani military rule, and press freedom was among their demands. He himself took part.

According to the author, the roughly 18 months of the interim government formed after the 2024 uprising did not live up to hopes. Under pressure, managements of media houses were changed, editors were removed, journalists lost jobs and self-censorship grew. In December 2025, after protests by hardline groups, Prothom Alo's office was set on fire and looted; he alleges that security forces were given no effective orders to stop it. The Daily Star's office was also surrounded and burned. The media reform commission's recommendations were left gathering dust.

He also looks back at the Awami League years: arrests of journalists, government advertisements cut off, about 50 companies made to stop advertising in 2015, nearly 80 cases against him and a case under the Digital Security Act. All of this is the author's own account.

In the February 2026 election the BNP returned to power after about 19 years. Rahman recalls that during the BNP's earlier terms he criticised it openly and did not face much trouble. In its 31-point reform programme and its manifesto, the party had promised a media commission, repeal of repressive laws and safety for journalists.

But seven months on, there has been no real reform. There are reports of interference in the management of some channels and newspapers, many journalists are writing in fear, and there is worry about a new cyber law. His conclusion is that the freedom to speak and publish is a right, not a concession handed out by those in power.
nazar: Rahman's experience shows that governments change, but the tools for tightening the grip on the press, like stopping advertisements, lawsuits and cyber laws, pass on to every new government. It is the same in India, and the biggest price is paid by the sections of society whose stories come out only through small, independent journalists.
sawal: Does any government ever stop fearing the press?
ref: Prothom Alo
Bangladesh's most widely read Bangla-language daily, edited by Matiur Rahman since 1998.
Digital Security Act
A 2018 Bangladeshi law that was used widely against journalists and critics; it was later replaced by a new law.

h: A court of delay: Jaffrelot and Dhawan question the Supreme Court
dek: In The Wire, Christophe Jaffrelot and Pranav Dhawan write that the court's delays in Election Commission cases and its silence on 10 October are weakening the rule of law.
body: This article by political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot and lawyer Pranav Dhawan links two things: the Supreme Court's tilted approach in electoral and constitutional cases, and its indifference to what the police and vigilante groups did on 10 October. According to them, reports in September revealed that the two election commissioners objected to the Chief Election Commissioner's decisions at least 14 times in ten months, while the 2023 law speaks of decisions by consensus or majority.

The court heard the petitions and asked the Commission for a reply, but refused an interim stay. According to the authors, the result is that the revision of the voter list goes on and scrutiny comes later. It also refused to hear quickly the case of voters in West Bengal with about 18,000 pending appeals.

Drawing on their own study of the court from 2014 to 2025, they say delay has been its favourite tool. The electoral bonds petition came in 2017 and the verdict in 2024, after several elections had passed. In 2023 a Constitution bench included the Chief Justice in the selection of commissioners; within a few months Parliament replaced him with a minister, and the court did not stay that law. They put this down to the government's influence over appointments and post-retirement posts.

The second part of the article alleges that on 10 October, vigilante groups linked to the Sangh Parivar (the family of Hindu nationalist organisations around the RSS) came out openly alongside the police, showed off weapons on social media and talked of targeting young protesters, yet the police gave them a free hand. The authors compare this to Sanjay Gandhi's squads during the Emergency.

Their demand is that the challenge to the 2023 law be sent to a Constitution bench and decided before next year's Assembly elections, and that voters with pending appeals be protected. In their view it is not enough to say that 'law and order is not a matter for the court'.
nazar: When the court delays, the burden falls first on those most at risk of having their names cut from the voter list: migrant workers, the poor, Muslims, Dalits and Adivasis, who are short of both papers and lawyers. The free hand given to vigilante groups is also the oldest and most bitter experience of these same communities.
sawal: Is justice delayed still justice when it comes to elections?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission's fresh check of the voter list, which faces allegations of names being cut on a large scale.
Shah Commission
The commission set up to inquire into the excesses of the Emergency (1975-77), headed by Justice J.C. Shah.

h: Ravi Nair's appeal: Gujarat High Court judge recuses himself
dek: Justice S V Pinto stepped away without giving reasons from the appeal of a journalist convicted in a defamation case linked to the Adani Group.
body: On Tuesday, 13 October, when independent investigative journalist Ravi Nair's appeal was called in the Gujarat High Court, Justice S V Pinto said the matter would not be heard in his court. According to The News Minute, he gave no reason. The appeal will now go to another bench, but the report does not say when or to whom.

Ravi Nair has done investigative reporting on several entities, including the Adani Group. The case concerns 16 of his posts on X made between October 2020 and July 2021, which the Adani side calls defamatory. At the start of the report the complaint is attributed to Adani Enterprises, while later it says the complaint was filed by an employee of Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone (APSEZ). According to the report, the posts were mostly based on stories published in places like The Guardian and NewsClick.

A magistrate's court in Gandhinagar convicted him of criminal defamation in February this year and sentenced him to one year. In March the sentence was suspended pending appeal. In September the sessions court sent him to jail over an alleged failure to appear, and he later got bail, as recorded in earlier LiveLaw reports.

Nair's lawyer Abhik Chimni has asked the court to admit additional evidence under Section 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. This evidence is the very news reports on which the tweets rested. In other words, the defence argues that the journalist was passing on information that had already been published.
nazar: A judge recusing is not wrong in itself, but without reasons, each time the appeal drags on longer, and the shadow of the sentence hangs over the journalist for that much longer. The fear that criminal defamation law becomes a tool in the hands of big companies to wear down critics seems to be coming true again and again.
Small and independent journalists have neither big lawyers nor an institutional shield. Cases like this also send other journalists a message to stay quiet.
sawal: How fair is a jail sentence for repeating a published story?
ref: Criminal defamation
In India, defamation can lead to a criminal case as well as a civil suit, with up to two years in jail. Press bodies have long demanded its removal.
Section 391, CrPC
If the court hearing an appeal thinks it necessary, it can order additional evidence to be taken or recorded.

h: Delhi protests case: Supreme Court hearing put off to Thursday
dek: Petitions alleging detentions, beatings and metro shutdowns were not argued on Tuesday, but several new matters were placed before the court.
body: Petitions challenging the action of police and paramilitary forces during the Delhi protests demanding the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation were before a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana on Tuesday. The petitions allege illegal detentions on a large scale, beating of protesters and arbitrary shutting of metro services.

The petitioners include CPI(M) general secretary M A Baby, RJD MP Manoj Kumar Jha, Professor Apoorvanand and several others. Menaka Guruswamy has filed a habeas corpus petition against the detentions, and the Supreme Court Bar Association has filed a separate petition over police action against lawyers. Some petitions allege contempt of the 9 October order that barred a complete shutdown of metro and train services.

As soon as the hearing began, several new matters were raised: a contempt petition by a journalist, a complaint of mistreatment of lawyers, and a case on violence against women journalists brought by Indira Jaising. According to LiveLaw, the Chief Justice asked for the women journalists' case to be listed the same day and for a senior government official to be present to respond.

Justice Mohana was sitting despite being unwell. For the petitioners, Gopal Sankaranarayanan himself suggested that since the arguments would be long, the hearing be moved ahead. The matter was put off until Thursday.
nazar: On Sunday the court had said clearly that peaceful people should not be illegally detained and that journalists' work should not be obstructed. If complaints are still coming in after that, the real question is whether the orders are being followed.
Those driven around in buses for hours included students, workers and women. For them, every postponed date is justice delayed.
sawal: How many days does a court order take to reach the street?
ref: Habeas corpus
A petition asking the court to have a detained person produced and the legal basis of the detention explained.

h: Instagram accounts of Journo Mirror and Molitics blocked in India
dek: Both digital media outlets say they got no warning beforehand and were not told under which order the action was taken.
body: The Instagram account of digital news outlet Journo Mirror has been blocked in India. The account carries a message that access has been temporarily restricted because of legal requirements under the country's IT rules. According to Maktoob, the account had about five lakh followers and its videos had been viewed 3.78 crore times in the past 30 days. Three days earlier, the Instagram account of Molitics India had been taken down.

Both outlets say they received no prior notice, and were not told the order or provision. Journo Mirror co-founder Mohammad Ali says he found out on returning from reporting on a protest. He suspects the reason may be their coverage of the protests demanding the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation. They will now carry on their work on other platforms such as Facebook.

Molitics editor Neeraj Jha said their Facebook page had also been shut down about six months ago, and since then Instagram had been their main platform. They are preparing to challenge the action in the High Court.

Meanwhile, Molitics reporter Aman Rastogi has filed a contempt petition in the Supreme Court. He alleges that despite the 11 October order, he was detained for two days even after showing his press card, and his phone was seized for about three hours and returned damaged.
nazar: Blocking accounts without giving reasons is the easiest censorship: no hearing, no accountability. Small outlets like these often carry the news of minorities, Dalits and marginalised people that the big channels miss.
If the order is lawful, why should there be any hesitation in making it public?
sawal: How do you challenge an order whose name you are never told?
ref: IT rules and blocking
Under Section 69A of the IT Act, the government can order content or accounts to be blocked; these orders usually stay confidential.

h: IIT Bombay: they spoke up on a Dalit student's death, and their Instagram was hacked
dek: The Ambedkar Periyar Phule Study Circle says its account was taken over right after it issued a statement on the death of a Dalit student.
body: Sahil Wakode, a Dalit student at IIT Bombay, died on 18 September. The campus student group Ambedkar Periyar Phule Study Circle (APPSC) has called it an institutional murder. According to the group, its Instagram account was hacked immediately after it issued a statement on this on 22 September, and it blames casteist forces. The Mooknayak has recorded this as the group's claim.

APPSC alleges that Professor Suryanarayana Doola, who held Wakode's last counselling session, had intimidated him, and that his parents had complained of caste-based harassment. These are allegations, not the findings of any inquiry. Some people linked to the institute have told the media there is no casteism on campus.

The group also says that through interim guidelines, reading caste-related books together on campus was banned. According to it, lights were switched off during public readings, videos were made without permission, and two students were suspended and thrown out of the hostel under these rules.

At the time of the report, Wakode's parents had been on hunger strike for 11 days. In their support, the All India Independent Scheduled Castes Association has called a protest at Mumbai's Azad Maidan on 16 October.
nazar: From Rohith Vemula to Darshan Solanki, every time the institutions first say there is no question of caste. When there are complaints that even reading Ambedkar is being restricted for students, this denial sounds even more hollow.
That a Dalit family has to go on hunger strike to get answers about their son's death says a lot about our biggest educational institutions.
sawal: Who is threatened by students reading Ambedkar together on campus?
ref: Rohith Vemula Act
The demand for a law to stop caste discrimination in higher education, raised after the death of University of Hyderabad research scholar Rohith Vemula in 2016.

h: Maharashtra drought: grape farmers fear 40 per cent losses
dek: Nashik got a third of its normal rain; in Solapur and Sangli some farmers will not be able to take a crop at all this time.
body: Nashik district received only 34.3 per cent of its normal southwest monsoon rain this year, and the monsoon withdrew about a month early. According to the Down To Earth report, grape growers fear losses of up to 40 per cent. Bajra (pearl millet), onion and other rain-fed crops are also being hit.

According to Kailas Bhosale, president of the Maharashtra State Grape Growers' Association, Solapur and Sangli are the worst affected, and some farmers there will not be able to take a crop at all this year. He says that if there is no water in 2027 either, the vines themselves could dry up. Planting a new vineyard costs at least five lakh rupees an acre, and the first crop comes after four years.

Vasantrao Dhikle, 59, of Pimpalgaon Baswant, says the late rain filled the ponds, which will keep the vines alive until the December-January harvest, but after that nobody knows. According to Bhosale, about 17 lakh farmers and farm workers depend on the state's grape trade.

Bharat Dighole of the onion growers' association believes onions get fewer pests in a drought, so some farmers may increase the area under onion to make up for losses. In a drought the irrigation department may give priority to drinking water, so Bhosale is asking for government help to save the vineyards.
nazar: Grapes are seen as a rich farmer's crop, but the blow falls first on farm workers, whose daily wages depend on harvesting and pruning. In a drought, work under the rural employment guarantee scheme is often their only support.
El Nino years are no longer the exception. Who comes first in sharing water, the vineyards, drinking water or small farmers, should be decided openly, starting now.
sawal: In a drought, should the first water go to the fields or to the village?
ref: El Nino
A warming of the Pacific Ocean that in India is often linked to a weak monsoon and a dry winter.

h: Pakistan Supreme Court: murder over a refused proposal shames society
dek: A three-judge bench dismissed a review petition seeking to reduce a death sentence, and made strong remarks on a woman's consent.
body: Pakistan's Supreme Court said on Tuesday that violence against a woman for refusing a marriage proposal is a deep stain on the conscience of society. A bench of Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar, Justice Salahuddin Panhwar and Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim dismissed Muhammad Kamran's review petition. The nine-page judgment was written by Justice Kakar.

Kamran had been convicted of murdering a woman after she and her family turned down his proposal. He has been on death row for about 15 years and had asked for his sentence to be commuted to life imprisonment. The court said that spending so many years does not automatically make someone equal to a prisoner serving a life term.

The court called absurd the argument that a refusal could be treated as provocation or a reason for leniency. According to the judgment, no one has the right to take a life because a proposal was turned down.

The judgment condemns customs such as ghag, swara and watta-satta, in which a woman's consent is treated as meaningless. The court recalled that free consent is essential for a valid nikah (marriage) in Islam, and also cited Article 16 of the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW).
nazar: This language, which gives full weight to a woman's 'no', is just as needed on this side of the border, where acid and knife attacks over one-sided love have become routine news.

Still, upholding the death sentence after 15 years on death row leaves the question of where the line between justice and revenge should be drawn. The real path to protecting women lies less in harsher punishment and more in changing customs.
sawal: When will society, and not just the law, accept a woman's 'no'?
ref: Swara and watta-satta
In swara a girl is handed over to settle a dispute; in watta-satta two families arrange marriages by exchanging daughters.
Ghag
A custom in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in which a man forcibly claims a woman for marriage; made a crime by a 2013 law.

h: Pakistan: government critic and anchor Iqrarul Hassan sent on remand
dek: His family alleges that men in plain clothes broke down the door of their home at three in the morning and took him away.
body: On Tuesday a judicial magistrate sent Pakistani TV anchor Iqrarul Hassan into four days' custody of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA). The agency alleges that he spread 'anti-state', false and defamatory content on his social media accounts. According to Dawn, these are the agency's allegations, not any finding of the court.

According to another Dawn report, Hassan has been criticising government policies on social media. His wife Farah Iqrar alleged in a video that at about three in the early hours of Monday, men in plain clothes broke down the main door of their home in Lahore's DHA and came in. According to her, a masked woman in the team was wearing an NCCIA tag, she was pushed around, and two mobile phones, a laptop and her own phone were also taken.

A few hours later, Punjab minister Azma Bokhari said the police had not arrested him and the matter was being investigated. According to lawyer Mian Ali Ashfaq, the NCCIA had also denied making the arrest.
Ashfaq says the anchor said nothing anti-state, and they were preparing to go to the Lahore High Court. First a denial, then remand by the same agency: this whole sequence is now under question.
nazar: Picking someone up in the middle of the night, denying it first and then producing them under a cyber law: this method is familiar to journalists across South Asia. In India too, vague charges like 'anti-national' against critical journalists have become common.
When social media posts themselves become crimes, every citizen who criticises those in power is a target.
sawal: Who decides, in the end, what counts as an 'anti-state' post?
ref: NCCIA
Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency, which investigates cases under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA).

h: Israeli raids in Ramallah target a prisoners' rights group and a women's committee
dek: The offices of Addameer and the Union of Palestinian Women's Committees were raided, and troops also entered the grounds of the largest government hospital.
body: On Tuesday the Israeli army raided the offices of two Palestinian non-governmental organisations in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank: the Union of Palestinian Women's Committees and Addameer, which works for prisoners. According to Al Jazeera correspondent Nida Ibrahim, Addameer's belongings were being seized.

The army also entered the grounds of the Palestine Medical Complex, described as the largest government hospital in the West Bank. According to the official news agency Wafa, snipers were deployed around the hospital gates. According to the Palestinian health ministry, a child was wounded by a bullet and several people suffered from suffocation during raids in Ramallah and al-Bireh.

Stun grenades were thrown at journalists covering the raid, and one journalist was injured by tear gas. According to Wafa, four photojournalists were detained in the Hebron area and stopped from reporting.

In 2021 Israel declared six Palestinian organisations, including these two, 'terrorist' groups and said they were branches of a left-wing faction. The organisations deny the charge. Addameer has been giving legal help to Palestinian prisoners since 1991.
nazar: A year after the 'ceasefire' in Gaza, organisations in the West Bank that speak up for the rights of prisoners and women are still under attack. Calling human rights groups 'terrorists' is an old way of crushing dissent.
India, which once stood openly with Palestine, now mostly stays silent on such actions.
sawal: What is there to fear from prisoners' lawyers?
ref: Addameer
A Palestinian organisation founded in 1991 that gives legal help to Palestinians held in Israeli prisons and documents torture in detention.

h: In Kashmir, apples replace paddy, and the rice on the plate comes from outside
dek: Valley farmers are planting apple orchards in paddy fields to earn more; a Mongabay India report shows the price is being paid by water, soil and food security.
body: In Qaimoh village in south Kashmir's Kulgam district, land where paddy swayed twenty years ago now has apple saplings standing on it. The irrigation channels built for paddy now water the orchards. According to the report, a farmer who earned 30 to 50 thousand rupees a year from nine kanals of paddy now gets four to five lakh rupees every season from apples.

Government figures show the change clearly. The area under paddy in the Valley fell from 3,04,500 hectares in 2015-16 to 2,58,840 hectares in 2024-25, a drop of about 15 per cent. Meanwhile the area under apples grew by about 60 per cent between 2004-05 and 2024-25. Kulgam now has 18,255 hectares under apples and only 6,951 hectares under paddy. The agriculture director admits that the department keeps no separate count of paddy land turned into orchards, and there is no specific policy to protect such land either.

The effect shows on the plate. Jammu and Kashmir produced about 6.5 lakh tonnes of rice in 2024-25, which by one agricultural scientist's estimate is 50-55 per cent of what it needs. The rest comes mainly from Punjab through the Food Corporation of India, and rice brought in from outside rose in two years from 3.74 lakh tonnes to 4.86 lakh tonnes.

There is also the question of water. Groundwater experts say paddy fields recharge shallow groundwater and hold back floodwater; orchards do not do this, which could increase flooding and waterlogging in the Jhelum plain. Recent hailstorms in Shopian and Kulgam ruined many orchards, in some places for the third time in a single season.

Economists are divided. One view is that Kashmir should specialise in apples, saffron, almonds and walnuts and buy rice. The other sees it as a structural risk: in a bad season both income and food take a hit at once, and turning an orchard back into a field is not easy.
nazar: This is not just Kashmir's story. When the market pushes farmers away from food crops towards cash crops and the government has neither data nor policy, the risk falls on the small farmer, who has no room to survive a single bad season. Growing dependence on Punjab means that if the road closes or the crop fails, poor households will be the first to see their rations shrink.
What is needed is not blaming farmers, but protecting key paddy land, bringing diversity into orchard crops and making sure rations are sufficient.
sawal: How secure will Kashmir be once it gives up its own rice?
ref: Kanal
A unit for measuring land in Kashmir; eight kanals make about one acre.
High-density orchard
Dwarf apple trees planted close together in a small space, which fruit earlier and more heavily.
SKUAST-K
Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology, Kashmir; the Valley's main agricultural university.

h: In the Matua heartland, the vote is gone and now there are queues for citizenship papers
dek: A PARI report: after names were cut during the SIR in North 24 Parganas, Matua families are paying for 'Hindu cards' and citizenship cards and waiting on the CAA.
body: On a Sunday in May 2026, Thakurbari, the religious centre of the Matua community in North 24 Parganas, was crowded, but not for worship. People were queueing for papers that might prove their citizenship. According to the report, more than 90 lakh names were cut in the state during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter list, and these people could not vote in the April 2026 Assembly election. The cuts were especially large in 15 Matua-majority seats.

Lalita Dhali, 43, from Kabilaspur, came about 30 kilometres on a scooty (scooter) with her husband Kartik. Kartik is a construction worker in Maharashtra and his name stayed on the list; Lalita's was cut. She paid 170 rupees for a 'Hindu card' and 500 rupees for a 'citizenship card', and is now thinking of applying under the CAA. Other families have spent anything from 200 to 850 rupees on such cards.

In Chikanpara village in Gaighata block, where many young men have gone away for work, the names of most Matua residents are lying 'under adjudication', and the booth level officers could not explain why. According to the report, more than 27 lakh people challenged the cuts in tribunals and still could not vote.

The Matuas are a Scheduled Caste community. In the late nineteenth century Harichand Thakur organised the Namasudras of eastern Bengal as an anti-Brahminical sect. After Partition many families came to India under duress and never had complete papers. The 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act offers a route to citizenship for religious minorities from Afghanistan, Pakistan and Bangladesh who arrived by 31 December 2014.

The community's leadership is also divided. Gaighata MLA Subrata Thakur calls the CAA the Matuas' shield, while Trinamool Rajya Sabha MP Mamata Bala Thakur told PARI that amid news of detention camps, many Matuas are afraid and confused.
nazar: This report shows that the burden of citizenship falls first on the shoulders of Dalits, migrants and people without papers. A community that political parties have treated as a vote bank for years saw its vote vanish in an administrative process, and is now paying money to prove who it is.

Most worrying is that women and workers employed outside the state seem to be caught more in this sorting. In a democracy, the duty of proving the right to vote should lie with the state, not the citizen.
sawal: Who will give back the vote to those who never had papers?
ref: Matua

h: Gaza: a journalist reporting on her own displacement
dek: A new film in Al Jazeera's Witness series follows Maram Humaid as the order comes to empty Gaza City and she and her family become part of the very crowd she is reporting on.
by: Mohammed Sawwaf, Salah al-Haw, Ibrahim al-Otla
body: This film, released on 12 October in Al Jazeera English's documentary series Witness, is about Gaza journalist Maram Humaid. Maram reports and writes from Gaza and gathers the stories of Palestinians living through the war. The film was made by Mohammed Sawwaf, Salah al-Haw and Ibrahim al-Otla.

At the centre of the film is the period when Israel ordered the whole of Gaza City to be emptied. According to the film's page, this was the first time in this war that an order came to evacuate an entire city, and for Maram these were among the hardest days of her life. After that order, reports of hundreds of thousands of people being pushed from north to south appeared around the world.

What sets the film apart is that this time the reporter is not watching from outside. Maram is recording the displacement and living it at the same time. She has a mother's responsibilities, food shortages, and grief over the deaths of fellow journalists. Through all this she keeps working, knowing it puts her life at risk.

Passing through the emptying city with her family, she meets people who decided to leave and also those who decided to stay. This choice between leaving and staying is the axis of the film: there is risk on both sides, and neither path is safe.

It is important to know the film's context. In this war, which began in October 2023, a large number of journalists have been killed in Gaza, and organisations that protect journalists have repeatedly called it the deadliest period for journalists on record. Foreign journalists were not allowed to enter Gaza freely, so most of the images that reached the world came through local journalists like Maram.

Witness is the Al Jazeera series that shows big stories through the eyes of one person. This film, too, moves less through figures or debate and more through one family's daily struggles, and that is what makes it worth watching.
nazar: In India we often see Gaza through the lens of diplomacy or religion. This film shows it through the eyes of a reporter who has neither a safe office nor a home to return to. It reminds us that the highest price for recording the truth is often paid by local, low-paid journalists, whether they are in Gaza or in Kashmir, Bastar and Manipur.
The pain of forced displacement does not see borders. Our own people who have lived through evictions, bulldozers and ruined neighbourhoods will recognise themselves in this film.
sawal: When the reporter is herself homeless, whose story is it?
ref: Witness
Al Jazeera English's documentary series, which shows films by independent filmmakers from around the world.
Gaza City
The largest city in the Gaza Strip, in the north; during the war, orders were repeatedly given to send people from here to the south.

h: From small towns to the classics: a young Carson in a 2002 conversation
dek: Shubh Chakraborty's translation on Anhad Kolkata: Will Aitken's 2002 conversation for The Paris Review, in which Anne Carson, long before the Nobel, talks about her childhood, her studies and the recognition that came late.
body: This conversation was done in 2002 for The Paris Review by Anne Carson's friend Will Aitken, and Anhad Kolkata published it in its translation section on 12 October in Shubh Chakraborty's Hindi translation. Yesterday we wrote about Carson's creative process and a 2023 conversation; this text takes us two decades back, to a poet the world did not yet properly know.

It starts with childhood. With the transfers of her father, who worked in a bank, the family kept moving from one Ontario town to another. Then come her studies in classics in Toronto and at St Andrews in Scotland, and her research on the ancient Greek poet Sappho, which became the ground for all her later work.

One part of the conversation is about the slow road to recognition. Her early books came out from small Canadian publishers, and her name was made quite late; later she also won the T.S. Eliot Prize. She speaks openly on the question of the personal and the impersonal in poetry, and her habit of often calling her poetry a 'failure' shows here too.

She sees ancient Greece neither as something directly useful for today's work nor as wholly foreign; for her it is a distance one can talk across. Towards the end there is a discussion of the book about her late brother Michael, built from Catullus's elegy and a cutting and joining of family photographs, and a mention of an opera-like work on three mystics that she was working on at the time.
nazar: In the flood of translations after the Nobel, this choice is useful because it shows Carson before fame: small publishers, slow recognition, and constant movement between scholarship and poetry. For Hindi writers who write with the support of little magazines and small presses, it is an important reminder that great work often ripens at the margins.
Our summary does not repeat the text of the translation. Read the full conversation on Anhad Kolkata; credit for the original interview goes to Will Aitken and The Paris Review.
sawal: Does great literature always grow on the strength of small publishers?
ref: Sappho
A Greek poet from around the sixth century BCE, whose poems survive mostly in fragments; Carson has also translated her.
Catullus
A poet of ancient Rome; his elegy on his brother's death is the basis of Carson's book about her brother.

h: Separating the art from the artist: a convenience for whom?
dek: Dharmesh Chaubey in Sammukh: Tanushree Dutta's allegations amid the mourning for Nana Patekar, the mocking of the trans community, and questions about the shield of the 'great artist'.
body: According to the article, the news of Nana Patekar's death brought a flood of tributes in the Hindi and Marathi cultural world. Dharmesh Chaubey does not deny the worth of his serious acting, but says praise cannot become an excuse to wipe out the rest of the record.

He recalls 2018, when Tanushree Dutta alleged sexual misconduct on a film set in 2008. According to the writer, Patekar did not lose work, the complaint was dismissed, and instead Tanushree faced threatening calls and lost work. The question is why our memory is so short.

The article then turns to the argument 'separate the art from the artist'. Chaubey says this argument often protects the powerful, while their violence falls on people at the margins. As examples he lists a Tamil domestic worker in Sri Lanka recorded in Neruda's memoir, J.K. Rowling's anti-trans campaign, Picasso, Naipaul and Polanski.

The sharpest part is about the trans and Kinnar (traditional transgender) communities. The writer points to scenes in 'Yeshwant' (1996) and 'Tum Milo Toh Sahi' (2010) that mocked this community, and links this to a long exclusion that began with the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871. The article also mentions Maddy Sandhu, a queer make-up artist who was killed in Amritsar.
The conclusion is clear: according to the writer, art is never separate from the artist, and those lost in mourning should also think about what they are looking away from.
nazar: This article is a reminder that 'greatness' is often counted at the cost of those whose voices are already weak: women, domestic workers, trans and Kinnar people. Even after MeToo, the worlds of cinema and literature have not built any system of accountability.
When someone dies, respect for their work and questions about their conduct can go together. The trouble starts when the second is drowned out by the noise of the first.
sawal: How much room should truth have in a tribute?
ref: MeToo (India)
A campaign that gathered force in India in 2018, in which women spoke openly about their experiences of sexual harassment at work.
Criminal Tribes Act 1871
A British-era law that declared many communities criminal by birth; the Kinnar community was also brought under it.
