h: Virenniyat 8: poems of brighter days in a city of shut metros
dek: Ayushman's report in Sammukh: eight poets at an event in memory of Viren Dangwal, and a frank note on the difference between writing a poem and reading it aloud.
body: The report opens with Delhi's unease. Ahead of a protest, metro stations were shut, trains cancelled and the internet cut overnight. Ayushman reads this as the act of a frightened state and says resistance will go on anyway.

In this atmosphere, the eighth 'Virenniyat' was held at Jawahar Bhawan. It is held in memory of the poet Viren Dangwal. Eight poets were invited. Ibbar Rabbi could not come because of illness, and Ashutosh Kumar read his poem about the buses used for detention.

The writer gives his view on each poet, with both praise and complaint. He found Arbaz Khan's poetry strong in places and slack in others; the pile-up of similes in Saumya Malviya's work jarred; in Chetan Kranti he saw today's politics and the discontent of the young. He sees Parvati Tirkey's Adivasi (indigenous) poetic vision as different from and more restrained than that of Jacinta Kerketta and Anuj Lugun. Savita Singh and Anamika raised the question of violence against women and of freedom, and according to the writer the most powerful reading was Anamika's.
One important point in the report is that writing a poem and reading it aloud are two separate arts. A weak reading spoils a good poem, and a good reading makes even a light poem shine.

At the end, Vir Bharat Talwar released Dangwal's selected collection 'Ujle Din Aayenge Zaroor' (Bright Days Will Surely Come), and people were seen rushing off before the metro closed at nine at night.
nazar: In the same week that the city's veins were being shut in Delhi to stop sit-ins and protests, poets sat in a room and spoke of detention, mosques, forests and women burned by acid. This is literature's old job: to record what power wants forgotten.
Having an Adivasi voice like Parvati Tirkey on the stage also matters, because the fight for land and forest is often missing from Delhi's debates.
sawal: When the city is shut down, who is poetry read for?
ref: Viren Dangwal
Hindi poet (1947-2015) who won the Sahitya Akademi Award for 'Dushchakra Mein Srashta' (The Creator in a Vicious Circle); he was closely tied to Bareilly.
Virenniyat
A poetry event held in Delhi every year in memory of Viren Dangwal.

h: From goddess to daughter: Durga in Bengal's Agomoni and Bijoya songs
dek: Baby Shaw in Hindwi Bela: from Ramprasad Sen to Nazrul, how Bengal's poets turned the ten-armed goddess into Uma, who comes home to her parents once a year.
body: In this part of the 'C/O Bengal' series, Baby Shaw tells the story of a fascinating change: the goddess who killed Mahishasura became, in Bengali homes, the daughter Uma, who comes to her parents' home once a year. Himalaya is an ordinary father, Menaka a Bengali mother longing for her daughter, and Shiva a son-in-law whom the mother-in-law does not trust.

The writer sees its roots in the earth and mother worship of the tribal and folk societies that came before the Aryans, which later merged with the Vedic stream to become the Shakta tradition. Agomoni songs are the joy of the daughter's arrival, and Bijoya songs the grief of her leaving.

The big names in this change appear in the article in order. Ramprasad Sen gave a language for sulking with, quarrelling with and chatting to the goddess. Kamalakanta Bhattacharya added psychological depth to Menaka's dreams and worries, and Dasharathi Ray caught the dramatic moment when the mother is confused to see the warrior goddess in place of her daughter.

The writer links these songs to the crumbling Bengal of the eighteenth century, when bitter realities like poverty, polygamy and step-relations entered the songs. Then come Michael Madhusudan Dutt, Rabindranath and Kazi Nazrul Islam; Nazrul made the goddess a symbol of social and political revolt, and went to jail for it.

The article ends in the home kitchen: fish, pulao, mishti doi (sweet curd), and after the farewell, the wait all over again. The writer asks whether seeing the goddess as a daughter is a lack of devotion, or the most beautiful form of humanity.
nazar: This article shows how ordinary people have shaped religion to the measure of their own joys and sorrows. At a time when there are attempts to cast festivals in a single colour and a single aggressive language, this homely goddess of Bengal, who weeps and sulks, is a reminder of a different, more human tradition.

Menaka's songs are really also the voice of married daughters and their mothers, whose bond with the parental home shrinks to a few days a year. The mention of Nazrul also shows how natural the place of a Muslim poet has been in this tradition.
sawal: Why does a tradition that sees the goddess as a daughter feel necessary today?
ref: Agomoni-Bijoya
Shakta songs of Bengal: Agomoni for the joy of Uma coming to her parents' home, Bijoya for the grief of her leaving on Dashami.
Ramprasad Sen
An eighteenth-century Bengali Shakta poet whose 'Ramprasadi' songs are still sung today.

h: Small reasons before the big worry of saving the country
dek: Atul Tiwari's satirical prose in Hindwi Bela: from Kanpur's afternoon nap to Mysore's Dussehra, reasons to save the country are found in cities and friends.
body: The piece runs as a list, where each sentence is a condition for how the country can be saved. It opens with satire: that one should not need a metaphor to understand a plain thing, that the team should be put above personal glory, and that rest should not be seen as a conspiracy against work.

Then come the cities. For each one there is a wish to give back a small, human thing: the afternoon nap to Kanpur, winter sunshine to Delhi, the right to get soaked without an umbrella to Mumbai, the slow pace of the tram to Kolkata, a path to the Khwaja's shrine free of touts to Ajmer, and a little progressiveness along with its oranges to Nagpur.

The writer's argument is that if there are many small reasons to save the country, the big worry can wait a little. He also pokes fun at the poetry of the eighties that was written so much out of concern for saving the country that those who came after were left with nothing but criticising it.

Under the shine of Digital India, the cashless economy, the caste census, semiconductors and AI, the same old potholes are shown. With the help of films like 'Deewaar', 'Swades' and 'Gangaajal', the writer says everyone needs the courage to recognise their own truth and stand by it.

The final answer is the simplest: the country will be saved when two friends share the rent of one room, hide money from each other at the end of the month and become friends again on the first. The piece ends with a memory of Kakori and Bismil.
nazar: In an age of loud nationalism, this prose brings the country down from slogans to the afternoon nap, the tram and the shared room. That is its politics: a country is made of porters, paan sellers, taxi drivers and people who live on rent, not of manifestos.
The mention of Kakori is a reminder that the freedom struggle too rested on friendship and trust, on the friendship of Bismil and Ashfaq that needs to be repeated in today's climate of hate.
sawal: What small thing should be given back to your city?
ref: Kakori incident
In 1925, revolutionaries of the Hindustan Republican Association looted a train carrying government treasure near Kakori; Bismil and Ashfaqulla Khan were hanged.

h: Meena Bazaar: from a royal covered market to cassette shops
dek: Musharraf Parvez in Janaki Pul: the history of the Chatta Bazaar in the Red Fort, where royal women once ran shops and Pakistani qawwali cassettes were later sold.
body: The article opens with a personal memory. As a teenager, the writer bought cassettes of Pakistani singers, and later videos of qawwalis, from the Meena Bazaar near the Jama Masjid. From there he turns to Old Delhi and the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb (the shared Hindu-Muslim culture) of the city Shah Jahan built.

According to the writer, Shah Jahan had heard of the covered markets of West Asia, and after seeing such a market in Peshawar he decided to build one like it for Delhi's heat. Mukarram Khan, who was overseeing work on the Red Fort, was given the task. It was called Bazaar-e-Musaqqaf, or the Chatta Bazaar.

There is also a description of its design: the entrance through the Lahori Gate, two sections joined by an open octagonal courtyard in the middle, and two floors. According to the writer, today shops run only on the ground floor, and the upper part is used as storage or rented out.

In the Mughal era this was not a market for common people. The article says royal women ran shops here, and goods like gold and silver, silk, shawls, saffron and musk were sold. Under the British it became a market for the army's needs, and after independence it was opened to all; now bangles, toys, watches and clothes are sold here.

The famous story of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal meeting at a bazaar is also in the article, though it is said to date from several decades before this Delhi bazaar was built. In the end the writer sees it as a bridge between the past and the present.
nazar: The history of Old Delhi is often either turned into romantic tales or there are attempts to erase it by calling it 'foreign'. This article is a reminder that these buildings are still the livelihood of small shopkeepers and craftspeople, who are rarely mentioned in debates about heritage.
There are some confusions about dates in the article, so we have kept the disputed details as the writer's own.
sawal: Where do shopkeepers and craftspeople fit in the protection of heritage?
ref: Chatta Bazaar
The covered market inside the Red Fort's Lahori Gate, built in the seventeenth century in Shah Jahan's time.
Meena Bazaar
A Mughal court tradition in which a special market was held for royal women; later the name was taken by many markets.
